source_text: I. Plerique Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae Calvino, & aliis qui cum eo in Religionis negotio sentiunt, tribuere solent quod ab homine tollant liberum arbitrium, eumque omni libertate in agendo spolient, aut saltem doceant in eo liberum Arbitrium per peccatum penitus amissum & extinctum fuisse. Istud videre est apud Bailium Jesuitam in Catechesi quam refutat Rivetus in summa Controversiarum Tract. 4. quaest. 4. Ubi disputat contra Reformatos, quasi liberum hominis arbitrium simpliciter negarent: & apud Martinum Becanum Jesuitam alterum qui dicit Lutheranos & Calvinistas affirmare per peccatum primi parentis penitus sublatum esse liberum arbitrium. In summa Theol. Scholast. Tract. 1. cap. 2. quaest. 9.
english: Most teachers of the Roman Church commonly accuse Calvin and those who share his religious position of removing free choice from man and stripping him of any freedom in what he does. At the least, they say, these men teach that sin destroyed free choice in man altogether.

One example is the Jesuit Bailly, in the catechism that Rivet answers in his Summary of Controversies (treatise 4, question 4). There Bailly argues against the Reformed as if they flatly denied that man has free choice.

Another is the Jesuit Martin Becanus. In his Summa of Scholastic Theology (treatise 1, chapter 2, question 9) he says that Lutherans and Calvinists hold that the sin of our first parent completely did away with free choice.

source_text: II. Sed constans est Reformatorum omnium sententia liberum arbitrium simpliciter consideratum, & secundum propriam naturam atque essentiam, esse aliquid quod a creatura rationali separari non potest: adeoque libere agendi facultatem ab homine per peccatum prorsus sublatam non fuisse: imo hominem per peccatum corruptum non minus libere agere quae agit, quam agebat ante peccatum: ac seu sibi relictus peccato indulgeat, id plane summa cum libertate facere; sive per gratiam motus & excitatus meliori vitae studeat, actus illius quoque liberos esse, neque per gratiae Dei efficaciam quicquam libertati voluntatis ejus praejudicari.
english: Yet all the Reformed consistently hold that free choice, taken simply and in its own nature and essence, cannot be separated from a rational creature. So sin did not wholly remove man's power to act freely.

Indeed, man corrupted by sin acts no less freely in what he does than he did before sin. If he is left to himself and gives way to sin, he does it with complete freedom. If grace moves and rouses him to pursue a better life, those acts are free too, and the efficacy of God's grace takes nothing away from his will's freedom.

source_text: III. Inter eos etiam constat liberum illud arbitrium quod ab homine inseparabile est, non esse actum, aut habitum aliquem, sed potius quandam animae facultatem: neque tamen isto nomine designari facultatem quandam, quae sit a mente & voluntate distincta; sed liberum arbitrium homini convenire, quatenus intellectu & voluntate praeditus est.
english: They also agree that the free choice which cannot be separated from man is not an act or a habit. It is rather a faculty of the soul.
Even so, the name does not mean some faculty distinct from mind and will. Man has free choice because he has an intellect and a will.

source_text: IV. Verum non explicant omnes eodem modo qua in re sita sit libertas, ratione cujus homo liber in agendo dicitur, & a qua denominatur liberum ejus arbitrium. Et primo quidem ex Reformatis non pauci, libertatem illam cujus respectu homo dicitur esse liberi arbitrii, nec servituti, nec necessitati simpliciter opponi docent, sed potius coactioni. Ac plerumque loquuntur quasi coactio sola libertatem perimeret, & libertatem describunt immunitatem a coactione.
english: They do not all explain in the same way what the freedom consists in that makes man free in acting and gives his choice the name free.

To begin with, a good many of the Reformed teach that the freedom by which man is said to have free choice is not set against bondage, or against necessity as such, but against compulsion. They mostly talk as if compulsion were the only thing that destroys freedom, and they describe freedom as exemption from compulsion.

source_text: V. Nec tamen eorum mens est quaecunque sponte, & non coacta agunt, agentia esse libera. Agnoscunt enim bruta sponte agere, & ea nihilominus libertate spoliant. Itaque ad libertatem praeterea requirunt, ut qui agit non simpliciter naturae impulsu ducatur; sed ex consilio & ratione agat. Adeoque ex eorum mente, plena libertatis definitio erit, siquis dicat illam esse immunitatem a coactione in eo qui agit ex rationis judicio.
english: They do not mean, though, that everything that acts of its own accord and without compulsion acts freely. They grant that animals act of their own accord, yet they deny them freedom.

So for freedom they also require that the agent not simply be driven by nature's impulse but act from deliberation and reason. On their view, then, the full definition of freedom is exemption from compulsion in an agent who acts on the judgement of reason.

source_text: VI. Sic Marcus Wendelinus Christianae Theologiae lib. 1. cap. 5. in explicatione Theseos 18. liberum arbitrium definit, Voluntatis affectionem, qua proprio suo motu, absque coactione, eligit, vel repudiat rem ab intellectu monstratam. Et huic quoque similis est definitio Zachariae Ursini, Est itaque, inquit, liberum arbitrium facultas, seu potentia volendi, aut nolendi, seu eligendi, aut repudiandi objectum ab intellectu monstratum, proprio motu, sine coactione. In explicationibus Catecheticis, parte 1. quaest. 8. num. 1.
english: Thus Marcus Wendelin, explaining thesis 18 in his Christian Theology (book 1, chapter 5), defines free choice as "a disposition of the will by which, moving itself and without compulsion, it chooses or rejects what the intellect sets before it."

Zacharias Ursinus gives a similar definition in his Catechetical Explanations (part 1, question 8, number 1): "Free choice, then, is a faculty or power of willing or not willing, of choosing or rejecting, an object that the intellect sets before it, by its own movement and without compulsion."

source_text: VII. Ex hac vero sententia sequitur libertatem proprie consistere in lubentia illa, qua voluntas intellectus judicium sequitur, non vero in aliqua voluntatis indifferentia, aut potestate quadam ad opposita, sine qua consistere potest voluntatis libertas; quamvis revera voluntas ad multos suos actus indifferenter se habeat, ut docet idem Wendelinus loco modo citato. Ubi postquam tradidit jam allatam definitionem liberi arbitrii, subjungit, Hoc in genere ad arbitrii libertatem sufficit: quod enim addunt nonnulli, per arbitrium liberum voluntatem sua natura manere idoneam ad oppositum, seu diversum eligendum, vel actionem suspendendam; ad liberum arbitrium in genere non pertinet. Quia libertas arbitrii consistit quoque sine indifferentia ad utrumque oppositum, quam contrarietatis libertatem appellant. Adeoque libertas quoque est, quae ad oppositorum alterutrum determinata est: qualis in beatis, qui libere agunt bene, ita ut per confirmationem in bono non possint male agere. Imo ne contradictionis quidem libertas simpliciter ad arbitrii libertatem est necessaria: quia libere Deum laudant Beati, qui tamen non possunt non laudare.
english: It follows from this view that freedom properly lies in the willingness with which the will follows the intellect's judgement. It does not lie in any indifference of the will or any power for opposites, since the will's freedom can exist without these, even though in fact the will is indifferent toward many of its acts. Wendelin teaches this in the same passage.

After giving the definition quoted above, he adds: "This is enough, in general, for freedom of choice. Some add that through free choice the will by its nature stays able to choose the opposite or something else, or to hold back from acting. That does not belong to free choice in general.

"For freedom of choice also exists without indifference to either of two opposites, which they call the freedom of contrariety. So it is also freedom when the will is fixed on one of two opposites. That is how it is with the blessed: they do good freely, yet being confirmed in good they cannot do evil.
"Indeed, not even the freedom of contradiction is strictly necessary to freedom of choice. The blessed praise God freely, and yet they cannot fail to praise him."

source_text: VIII. Quamvis igitur ille, & qui cum eo sentiunt, agnoscant discrimen esse inter actus voluntatis, nempe ad quosdam voluntatem determinatam esse, aliorum vero respectu natura sua manere idoneam ad opposita; censent tamen voluntatem, tam horum quam illorum respectu, liberam dici debere, & tam hos quam illos libere a voluntate prodire & elici. Ac proinde distinguunt quidem inter voluntarium simpliciter, & illud quod fit ex electione: sed inter voluntarium & liberum non distinguunt. Nam utrumque volunt aeque late patere, & quicquid voluntarium est, hoc ipso esse liberum. Nec ullam necessitatem quae voluntarii naturam non evertat, libertatis naturam evertere existimant. Adeoque quamvis Deus per naturam bonus sit, docent tamen illum esse libere bonum, quoniam non coacte, sed voluntarie bonus est. Sicuti videre est apud Zachariam Ursinum loco jam allegato. Liberum, inquit, vocatur ἑκούσιον, hoc est, spontaneum: quod opponitur ἀκουσίῳ, hoc est, involuntario, & coacto: non autem ἀναγκαίῳ, seu necessario. Potest enim ἑκούσιον consistere cum ἀναγκαίῳ, sed non cum ἀκουσίῳ, ut Deus & sancti Angeli ἀναγκαίως, hoc est, necessario sunt boni: non tamen ἀκουσίως, hoc est, coacte, sed liberrime: quia principium suae bonitatis habent in seipsis, liberam voluntatem.
english: He and those who agree with him admit a difference among the will's acts: the will is fixed on some of them, while toward others it stays by nature able to go either way. Still they hold that the will should be called free with respect to both kinds, and that both kinds come freely from the will.

So they do distinguish between what is simply voluntary and what comes from choice, but they draw no line between the voluntary and the free. They want the two to cover the same ground, so that whatever is voluntary is free for that very reason. They do not think any necessity destroys the nature of freedom unless it also destroys the nature of the voluntary.

They therefore teach that God, though good by nature, is freely good, because his goodness is not forced but willed. Ursinus says this in the passage cited above: "What is free is called hekousion, that is, spontaneous. It is the opposite of akousion, the involuntary and forced, but not of anankaion, the necessary.

"Hekousion can go with anankaion, but not with akousion. God and the holy angels are good anankaios, that is, necessarily, yet not akousios, that is, under force; they are good most freely, because the source of their goodness is in themselves, a free will."

source_text: IX. Alii vero diserte & distincte affirmant, libertatem illam a qua homo liber in agendo dicitur, non esse immunitatem a sola coactione, quae est necessitas quam infert vis agentis externi, contra inclinationem illius quod cogi dicitur: sed libertatem illam opponi praeterea necessitati naturali, sive determinationi per naturam ad unum. Porro necessitas illa, quam naturalem vocant, a materia juxta ipsos oritur, idque duplici modo. Vel enim actio externa non dependet ab ulla actione interna a qua imperetur: sed posita facultate, & objecto materiali extrinsecus admoto, non potest non exerceri actio, & quidem talis, tantaque. Cui necessitati subjiciuntur, quaecunque sensu & ratione carent. Vel pendet quidem actio externa ab internae imperio, ut & suspendi possit, & non eodem modo semper fieri, sed tamen non nisi a re aliqua materiali determinatio oritur: sicuti contingit in brutis, quorum actiones externae a sensu pendent atque imperantur, & magnam varietatem, etiam circa unum & idem objectum admittunt, prout sensus eorum varie, tum interne, tum externe afficiuntur; sed ipsi eorum sensus ab objecto aliquo materiali semper moventur & determinantur. Homo vero ab utraque ista necessitatis specie immunis est. Nec enim in actibus illis, quorum respectu dicitur liberi esse arbitrii, a materia externe admota, aut etiam a solo materiali sensu in agendo determinatur. Sed cum sit agens intellectualis, agit atque appetit ex judicio atque imperio rationis.
english: Others state plainly and precisely that the freedom by which man is called free in acting is not exemption from compulsion alone, compulsion being the necessity imposed by an outside agent's force against the inclination of the thing compelled. That freedom, they say, is also opposed to natural necessity, that is, to being fixed by nature on one outcome.

This natural necessity, on their account, comes from matter, and in two ways. In one, the outward action does not depend on any inner act that commands it. Once the faculty is there and a material object is brought to it from outside, the action must take place, and with just this character and this strength. Everything without sense and reason is subject to this necessity.

In the other, the outward action does depend on an inner command, so that it can be held back and need not always happen the same way, yet what settles it comes only from something material. That is the case with animals. Their outward actions depend on sense and are directed by it, and they vary a great deal even toward one and the same object as their senses are affected in different ways, inwardly and outwardly. But their senses themselves are always moved and settled by some material object.

Man is free of both kinds of necessity. In the acts for which he is said to have free choice, he is not settled in acting by matter brought to him from outside, or even by material sense alone. Being an intellectual agent, he acts and desires on the judgement and command of reason.

source_text: X. Qua in re libertatem arbitrii constituunt. Idque quoniam illi qui ex judicio rationis agunt finis notitiam habent, eumque sibi praestituunt, & ad eum actiones suas dirigunt atque accommodant: & ita sunt quodammodo actionum suarum Domini. Cum contra res inanimae, & animalia bruta quae solo sensu ducuntur, finem suum non cognoscant; ideoque ad eum seipsa non referant, sed duntaxat ad illum tendant instar mancipiorum, imperata quidem facientium, cur vero imperentur, aut quorsum ignorantium. Neque tam propter finem agunt, quam ad finem ab agente superiore aguntur. Adde quod brutorum sensus & appetitus rebus materialibus astrictus est; hominum vero voluntas, cum sequatur ductum mentis & rationis, quae pro objecto habet non tantum sensibilia, sed etiam intelligibilia, non solum praesentia, sed etiam futura, versatur circa omnia bonorum genera, modos atque gradus, nec ullis, ut sic dicam, limitibus includitur: Unde nascitur maxima appetitionum electionumque necnon actionum externarum varietas.
english: This is where they locate freedom of choice. Those who act on reason's judgement know their end, set it before themselves, and direct and fit their actions to it, so that in a sense they are masters of what they do.

Lifeless things and animals that are led by sense alone, by contrast, do not know their end. So they do not direct themselves to it but only move toward it like slaves, who carry out orders without knowing why they are given or what they are for. They do not so much act for an end as get moved toward an end by a higher agent.

Besides, the sense and appetite of animals are tied to material things. Human will follows the lead of mind and reason, whose objects are not only things of sense but things of the intellect, not only present things but future ones. It ranges over every kind, mode and degree of good and is shut in, so to speak, by no limits. From this comes the great variety in what men desire and choose, and also in their outward actions.

source_text: XI. Quae latius diducta videre licet apud Josuam Placeum ante paucos annos in Academia Salmuriensi Professorem, tractatu de libero hominis Arbitrio. Ubi sic concludit ea quae pluribus ante hac de re disseruit. In eo igitur consistit naturalis voluntatis libertas, quod cum a coactione, & necessitate materiae, & rerum sensibilium sit libera, tam immaterialia quam materialia, tam intelligibilia quam sensibilia, tam futura quam praesentia, tam honesta quam utilia, aut jucunda, horumque contraria, omnes adeo bonorum & malorum ordines, gradus, relationes pro objecto habere possit omni loco & tempore, finem ultimum, fines intermedios, ad eosque conducentia media eligere potest pro arbitrio, hoc est, mentis practicae judicio, sine qua ne rationalis quidem est, nedum libera. Et postea repetit ex sua sententia non omnem necessitatem cum voluntate, id est, cum libertate arbitrii pugnare, sed eam duntaxat quae vel a coactione est, vel a materia sine sensu, vel a sensu sine ratione. Item, libertatem sitam esse in immunitate a triplici necessitate, coactionis nempe, determinationis a materia, & determinationis a sensu.
english: This is set out more fully by Josué de la Place, professor at the Academy of Saumur a few years ago, in his treatise On Man's Free Choice. There he sums up what he had argued at length before: "The natural freedom of the will consists in this. Being free of compulsion and of the necessity of matter and of things of sense, it can take as its object, in any place and at any time, things immaterial as well as material, of the intellect as well as of sense, future as well as present, honourable as well as useful or pleasant, and their opposites, in short every order, degree and relation of goods and evils.

"It can choose the final end, the intermediate ends and the means that lead to them as it judges fit, that is, by the judgement of the practical mind. Without that judgement it would not even be rational, let alone free."

Later he repeats, as his own view, that not every necessity clashes with the will, meaning with freedom of choice, but only the necessity that comes from compulsion, or from matter without sense, or from sense without reason. Likewise he says freedom lies in exemption from three necessities: compulsion, being settled by matter, and being settled by sense.

source_text: XII. Sed sunt qui ad libertatem actionum humanarum putant non sufficere immunitatem a coactione, & a necessitate determinationis a materia vel a sensu; sed libertatem illam praeterea excludere necessitatem quamlibet naturalem, etiamsi a materia, vel a sensu non oriatur. Nec etiam, ut actio libera sit, satis esse existimant, ut homo quovis modo ex judicio rationis agat; ad hoc etiam requiri tale judicium quod sit conclusio cujusdam deliberationis, & consultationis; adeoque illa solum libere a nobis fieri, de quibus consultare & deliberare licet. Ac proinde cum sint quidam voluntatis nostrae actus ad quos per naturam determinata est, & circa quos nemo unquam consultat atque deliberat, qualis est actus ille quo beati esse volumus, & nolumus esse miseri, circa hos voluntatem liberam esse non sentiunt: nec etiam ad modum causae liberae se habere, respectu motuum illorum qui in voluntate subito excitantur, ex perturbatione aliqua vehementi, priusquam mens nostra seipsam colligere potuerit, & deliberationem aliquam instituere. Unde est quod distinguunt inter liberum & voluntarium, & statuunt voluntarium latius patere quam liberum: cum voluntarium omne liberum non sit.
english: Some, however, think that exemption from compulsion and from being settled by matter or sense is not enough for human actions to be free. In their view freedom also rules out every kind of natural necessity, even one that does not come from matter or sense.

Nor do they think it enough for a free action that a man act on reason's judgement in any way at all. The judgement must be the conclusion of some deliberation and weighing. Only those things are done freely by us, then, about which we can take counsel and deliberate.

Now there are some acts of our will to which it is fixed by nature and about which no one ever deliberates, such as the act by which we want to be happy and do not want to be miserable. They do not hold that the will is free in these. Nor do they think it acts as a free cause in the impulses that rise in it suddenly from some violent disturbance before our mind can collect itself and begin to deliberate.
That is why they distinguish the free from the voluntary and hold that the voluntary is the wider class, since not everything voluntary is free.

source_text: XIII. Haec est doctrina Andreae Riveti olim in Academia Leydensi Professoris Summae Controversiarum tract. 4. quaest. 3. Libertatis rationem agnoscimus, inquit, consistere non posse, non solum cum coactione proprie dicta, sed etiam cum necessitate naturali, qua agens ad unum natura determinatum est; nec sufficere ad libertatem si homo sponte aliquid faciat, quod etiam causis naturalibus competit, sed necessariam esse deliberationem praeviam, & rationis judicium, quae locum non habent ubi est determinatio ex naturae necessitate. Et postea, Nos, inquit, in libertate haec tria distinguimus, quibus liberi arbitrii naturam per se explicamus. 1. Ut sit libertas in subjecto, nempe in voluntate, quae ex principio suo interno, sine discursu & consilio, agit semper sponte citra coactionem; sed cum consilio & deliberatione libere citra necessitatem. Sine prima libertate a coactione destruitur natura voluntatis, cui necessitas imponitur ut cogi non possit in actu suo, ut vocant, elicito. Sine deliberatione autem ex indifferentia intellectus, libere velle non potest, nempe si natura ad unum determinata esset. Et propterea liberum arbitrium cum Thoma dicit esse vim electivam. Et cum Bellarmino agnoscit ad essentiam liberi arbitrii pertinere, ut quis habeat optionem diversarum rerum, & electio fiat cum pleno atque perfecto rationis judicio.
english: This is the teaching of Andrew Rivet, formerly professor at the Academy of Leiden, in his Summary of Controversies (treatise 4, question 3): "We acknowledge that the nature of freedom cannot coexist with compulsion in the proper sense, nor with natural necessity either, by which an agent is fixed by nature on one outcome. It is not enough for freedom that a man does something of his own accord, since natural causes do that too. Prior deliberation and a judgement of reason are required, and these have no place where nature's necessity settles the act."

Later he says: "We distinguish three points in freedom, by which we explain the nature of free choice in itself. 1. Freedom is in a subject, namely the will. Acting from its own inner principle without reasoning or deliberation, the will always acts of its own accord and without compulsion; acting with counsel and deliberation, it acts freely and without necessity.

"Without the first freedom, from compulsion, the nature of the will is destroyed, for necessity is laid on the will that it cannot be forced in what they call its elicited act. Without deliberation arising from the intellect's indifference, it cannot will freely, since it would then be fixed by nature on one outcome."

So with Thomas he calls free choice an elective power. And with Bellarmine he grants that it belongs to the essence of free choice that one has the option between different things and that the choice is made with a full and complete judgement of reason.

source_text: XIV. Similis est hac in parte Doctrina Mosis Amyraldi nuper in Academia Salmuriensi Professoris Tractatu de libero hominis arbitrio, p. 61. & seqq. Ubi primo distinguit duplicem voluntatis motionem. Unam quae non est sejuncta quidem ab ea cognitione quae a ratione ducit originem, sed est istiusmodi tamen ut cognitio ex qua nascitur ac efflorescit, non sit ipsa orta ex praevia consultatione: alteram quae non modo conjuncta est cum aliqua cognitione, sed nascitur ex ea notitia quam προβούλευσις, i. e. consultatio antecessit, & quae nihil aliud est quam Conclusio quae ex deliberatione conficitur, consideratis, scilicet, atque comparatis inter se pluribus objectis, aut uno & eodem objecto spectato diversimode, adeo ut mens aliquandiu hinc & illinc rationum librata ponderibus, tandem in unam partem inclinetur. Deinde observat illam voluntatis motionem, quae nullam mentis consultationem & deliberationem sequitur, adhuc duplicem esse, nimirum voluntatem per unam in finem, id est, beatitudinem & felicitatem ipsam ferri; per alteram in media quae ad finem istum ducere existimantur.
english: Moses Amyraut, until recently professor at the Academy of Saumur, teaches much the same on this point in his treatise On Man's Free Choice (p. 61 and following). He first distinguishes two movements of the will.

One is not cut off from the knowledge that has its source in reason, but the knowledge from which it springs and grows did not itself come out of any prior weighing. The other is not only joined with knowledge but arises from knowledge that consultation (probouleusis) went before. That knowledge is simply the conclusion reached by deliberation, when several objects are considered and compared, or one and the same object is looked at in different ways, so that the mind, swung this way and that for a while by the weight of reasons, finally leans to one side.

Next he observes that the movement of the will that follows no weighing or deliberation by the mind is itself of two kinds. By one the will is carried toward the end, namely happiness and blessedness itself; by the other toward the means thought to lead to that end.

source_text: XV. Postea vero neutram istarum motionum ad liberum arbitrium pertinere ostendit. Non priorem, quia liberum arbitrium est id quod Aristoteles προαίρεσιν appellavit. Jam vero, inquit, προαίρεσιν omnem antecedit aliqua προβούλευσις. Nemo autem de extremo illo fine consultat, sed fertur in eum non necessario duntaxat, sed etiam ἀπροβουλεύτως. Non etiam superiorem, quia etsi motus iste a superiori differat, est etiam cum eo aeque ἀπροβούλευτος. Siquidem usque adeo subitus est, usque adeo velociter, vel ex perturbatione aliqua ortus, vel ex ingentis alicujus & improvisi atque inopinati objecti praesentia natus erumpit, ut omnem consultationem antevertat. Unde colligit motum ejusmodi esse quidem ἑκούσιον, id est, spontaneum & voluntarium, non autem προαιρετικόν, id est, liberum atque electivum. Ac propterea recte dici solere primos passionum nostrarum impetus non esse in nostra potestate; quoniam ea sola sunt in nostra potestate de quibus consilium capimus, an sint a nobis, vel usurpanda, vel omittenda: ac proinde quae omnem deliberationem praecurrunt, illa in potestate nostra esse non arbitramur. Unde tandem concludit pag. 65. Restat ergo ut ad arbitrium nostrum pertinere putentur ea de quibus deliberare possumus, utque illa itidem ex arbitrio nostro libero profecta esse dicamus de quibus ita deliberavimus, ut deliberationem & consultationem secuta sit appetitio: qua in re τὴν προαίρεσιν, jam saepe sitam esse diximus.
english: Then he shows that neither movement belongs to free choice. Not the first, because free choice is what Aristotle called prohairesis, and as he says, "every prohairesis is preceded by some probouleusis. No one deliberates about that final end; one is carried toward it not only by necessity but without any prior deliberation (aprobouleutos)."

Not the second either: though it differs from the first, it is just as much without prior deliberation. It is so sudden and so quick, whether it comes from some disturbance or bursts out at the sight of something great, unforeseen and unexpected, that it gets ahead of all weighing. He infers that such a movement is indeed hekousion, spontaneous and voluntary, but not prohairetikon, free and elective.

This is why it is rightly said that the first stirrings of our passions are not in our power. Only the things we take counsel about, whether we should take them up or leave them alone, are in our power, and we do not count as in our power what runs ahead of all deliberation.

So at last he concludes (p. 65): "What belongs to our choice, then, must be the things we can deliberate about. And we should say that those things come from our free choice which we have deliberated about in such a way that desire followed the deliberation and weighing. That, as we have often said, is where prohairesis lies."

source_text: XVI. Sed praeter necessitatem quae est a coactione, a materia, vel a sensu, aut a quavis alia naturae determinatione, quaedam necessitas est quae concipitur oriri ab aliqua causa externa, velut ab ipso Deo, sic facultatem ipsam movente atque impellente, ut veram imponat agendi necessitatem, id est, ab agente tollat potestatem aliter agendi; licet qui agit supponatur agere sponte, & non invitus. Quam necessitatem Scholae motivam atque impulsivam vocant. Non desunt autem inter Reformatos, qui hanc quoque necessitatem cum humana libertate pugnare existiment, quique putent cum ea consistere non posse ullam proprie dictam necessitatem, quae in Scholis appellatur necessitas consequentis, opposite ad necessitatem quae consequentiae dicitur.
english: Beyond the necessity that comes from compulsion, from matter, from sense or from any other settling by nature, there is a necessity thought to come from an outside cause, God himself for instance, moving and driving the faculty in such a way that he lays on it a true necessity of acting. That is, he removes from the agent the power to act otherwise, even though the agent is supposed to act of his own accord and not unwillingly. The schools call this motive or impulsive necessity.

Some among the Reformed think that this necessity too clashes with human freedom. They hold that freedom cannot coexist with any necessity in the proper sense, what the schools call necessity of the consequent, as opposed to necessity of the consequence.

source_text: XVII. Haec est sententia Gulielmi Amesii olim in Academia Franekerana Theologi, Nos, inquit, concedimus liberum arbitrium, in eo quod agit liberum esse ab omni necessitate, ut proprie non possit necessario agere quoad exercitium sui actus, quamvis respectu divinae ordinationis certo & infallibiliter agat. In Bell. Enervato tom. 4. lib. 4. cap. 1.
english: William Ames, formerly theologian at the Academy of Franeker, takes this view. In his Bellarmine Disarmed (volume 4, book 4, chapter 1) he writes: "We grant that free choice, in what it does, is free from all necessity.
"Properly speaking it cannot act by necessity as regards the exercise of its act, even though, with respect to God's ordaining, it acts certainly and infallibly."

source_text: XVIII. Idem quoque sentit Rob. Baronius olim in Academia Abredonensi Professor in Metaphysica sua generali ad Theologiae usum accommodata, ubi inter alia multa haec duo asserit, Primo voluntatem in suis actionibus eliciendis non teneri, vel constringi necessitate absolute dicta, quam appellant necessitatem consequentis. Deinde voluntatem, etiam hominis lapsi, nulla necessitate motiva, vel impulsiva teneri respectu Dei. Ille etiam, inquit, hominibus liberum arbitrium dedit, & per consequens non tollit totaliter eam facultatem, ei imponendo necessitatem, aut per decretum suum aeternum, aut per temporariam motionem, & inflexionem. Sect. 12. Disp. 1. de libertate Arbitrii num. 17.
english: Robert Baron, formerly professor at the Academy of Aberdeen, holds the same in his General Metaphysics Adapted to the Use of Theology. Among much else he makes two claims there.

First, the will is not held or bound, in producing its acts, by necessity in the absolute sense, what they call necessity of the consequent. Second, the will, even of fallen man, is not held by any motive or impulsive necessity with respect to God.

"He too," Baron says, "gave men free choice. So he does not do away with that faculty entirely by laying necessity on it, either through his eternal decree or through a motion and bending in time." (Section 12, Disputation 1, On Freedom of Choice, number 17.)

source_text: XIX. Ut autem quid mihi quoque videtur aperiam, existimo primam sententiam quae libertatem definit immunitatem a coactione in eo qui agit ex judicio rationis, reipsa non differre a secunda sententia, quae libertatem opponit non tantum coactioni, sed etiam necessitati quae a materia vel a sensu oritur, quam alii Physicam necessitatem vocant. Quandoquidem enim statuit immunitatem a coactione non esse dignam nomine libertatis, nisi in eo qui ratione utitur; evidenter supponit ad libertatem requiri, ut agens rationis judicium sequatur, non vero a materia, vel a sensu determinetur. Adeoque haec secunda sententia a priori non differt, nisi quod proponitur distinctius & explicatius.
english: To give my own view as well: I think the first opinion, which defines freedom as exemption from compulsion in an agent acting on reason's judgement, does not differ in substance from the second, which opposes freedom not only to compulsion but also to the necessity that comes from matter or sense, called by some physical necessity.

The first opinion holds that exemption from compulsion does not deserve the name of freedom except in a being that uses reason. Plainly, then, it assumes that freedom requires the agent to follow reason's judgement and not to be settled by matter or sense. So the second opinion differs from the first only in being stated more precisely and more fully.

source_text: XX. In utraque autem istud incommodi est quod omnino confundunt liberum & voluntarium, & statuunt omnes actus voluntatis liberos esse. Nam juxta sensum communem hominum, & receptum loquendi usum, istud solum liberum nobis esse dicitur, quod in nostra potestate est, quod potest aliter se habere, & de quo nobis consultare & deliberare licet. Jam vero, ut supra ostendimus, sunt quidam voluntatis actus, ad quos per naturam sic determinata est, ut nullo modo possint aliter se habere, & de quibus nulla potest institui deliberatio. Adde quod omnes actus qui a nobis libere procedunt possunt praeceptis quibusdam subjacere, & lege aliqua divina, vel humana mandari, sive prohiberi. Istud autem nullo modo convenit iis actibus circa quos voluntas plane immutabiliter se habet, ita ut in nullo statu potuerit, vel possit unquam aliter agere. Denique cum illi quibuscum nobis res est, fateantur & agnoscant magnum discrimen esse inter actus voluntatis, nempe quosdam sic esse in nostra potestate, ut de iis possimus consultare & deliberare; illosque pro vario mentis practicae judicio, vel facere, vel omittere, aut etiam contrarium agere; aliorum vero plane diversam esse rationem; cur nolunt res natura distinctas, distinctis quoque vocibus signare, & juxta usum in Scholis receptum illis quidem liberi, his vero voluntarii nomen appropriare? cum sapientis sit sine necessitate a communi loquendi modo non recedere.
english: Both views share one drawback: they wholly confuse the free with the voluntary and hold that every act of the will is free. In the common understanding of men and in ordinary usage, we call free only what is in our power, what could be otherwise, and what we are allowed to weigh and deliberate about.

But as shown above, there are acts of the will to which it is so fixed by nature that they cannot be otherwise in any way, and about which no deliberation can be held. Further, every act that comes from us freely can fall under precepts and be commanded or forbidden by some law, divine or human. That does not fit at all the acts toward which the will stands quite unchangeably, so that in no state could it, or ever can it, act otherwise.

Lastly, the men we are dealing with admit a great difference among the will's acts. Some are in our power, so that we can weigh and deliberate about them and, as the practical mind judges one way or another, do them, leave them undone, or even do the opposite; the others are of a quite different kind. Why, then, will they not give things that differ in nature different names too, and, following the usage of the schools, reserve 'free' for the first and 'voluntary' for the second? A wise man does not leave the common way of speaking without need.

source_text: XXI. Caeterum inter Doctos illos viros qui liberum & voluntarium confundere videntur, nonnulli sunt qui monent libertatem voluntatis, sive liberum Arbitrium duplici modo sumi, late, scilicet, & stricte. Libertas voluntatis in genere, sive late sumpta, juxta ipsos, nihil aliud est quam τὸ ἑκούσιον νοητικόν, spontaneum intellectuale, id est, spontaneum praeeunte intellectus lumine, vel judicio. Adeoque in hoc proprie consistit generalis ista voluntatis libertas, quod voluntas hactenus Dominium sui actus habeat, ut nequaquam cogi possit, sed pro libito, ex certa ratione, consideratione, aut judicio, sese moveat, & cohibeat, agat, aut non agat.
english: Among the learned men who seem to confuse the free and the voluntary, some point out that freedom of the will, or free choice, is taken in two ways, a broad one and a strict one.

Freedom of the will in general, or in the broad sense, is for them nothing but to hekousion noetikon, intellectual spontaneity, that is, spontaneity led by the light or judgement of the intellect. This general freedom of the will properly consists in the will's having mastery over its act to the extent that it can never be forced. Instead it moves or restrains itself, acts or refrains, as it pleases, for some definite reason, consideration or judgement.

source_text: XXII. Haec est illa libertas, quam ex eorum sententia, voluntas in omnibus suis actionibus exercet, idque non tantum quum versatur circa media ad finem spectantia, aut ea quae parum, aut nihil ad finem conducunt, sed etiam, quum versatur circa ipsum finem. Ac proinde ipsa necessitas quae voluntatis naturam sequitur, eique consentanea est, & per quam determinata est ad summum finem prosequendum, hanc voluntatis libertatem minime evertit, aut minuit.
english: This, in their view, is the freedom the will exercises in all its acts. It does so not only when dealing with the means to the end, or with things that contribute little or nothing to the end, but also when dealing with the end itself.
So the necessity that flows from the will's nature and agrees with it, by which the will is set on pursuing the highest end, in no way destroys or lessens this freedom of the will.

source_text: XXIII. Strictius vero usurpata libertas, sive liberum arbitrium restringitur, ipsis fatentibus ad media relata ad finem, aut ad ea quae parum, aut nihil ad finem conducunt, & versatur circa τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, id est, circa ea quae sunt in nostra potestate, & recte ab Aristotele definitur spontaneum ex praevia deliberatione ortum, sive Deliberativa appetitio eorum quae sunt in nostra potestate. Quo in sensu liberi actus dicuntur qui sunt mere contingentes, & qui a nobis pro arbitrio fieri possunt, aut non fieri. Eoque respectu libertas includit quandam indifferentiam, neque aliter voluntas libera est quam quatenus est indifferens, nempe, cum possit circa idem objectum agere, vel non agere, & cum possit tam illud, quam aliud, aut ejus oppositum eligere. Et hoc sensu Deus libere se non amat, quia naturae necessitate seipsum vult & amat; nec etiam homo libere vult esse foelix, & non vult esse miser, quia sic vult & non aliter per naturalem quandam necessitatem.
english: Freedom in the stricter sense, or free choice, is by their own admission limited to means directed to the end, or to things that contribute little or nothing to it. It concerns ta eph' hemin, the things in our power, and Aristotle rightly defines it as the spontaneous arising from prior deliberation, or deliberative desire for things in our power.

In this sense acts are called free when they are purely contingent and we can do them or not do them as we choose. Taken so, freedom includes a kind of indifference. The will is free only in so far as it is indifferent, that is, able to act or not act toward the same object, and able to choose this, or something else, or its opposite.

In this sense God does not love himself freely, since he wills and loves himself by the necessity of his nature. Nor does man freely want to be happy and not want to be miserable, since he wills this, and cannot will otherwise, by a natural necessity.

source_text: XXIV. Haec est doctrina Johannis Strangii, S. S. Theologiae Doctoris & Professoris primarii in Academia Glasguensi, Tractatu de voluntate & actionibus Dei circa peccatum, lib. 3. cap. 14. Ubi postquam haec quae diximus exposuit & latius diduxit, dicit se non negare vocem liberi arbitrii stricto illo sensu recte usurpari, quanquam in alio & latiori sensu affirmet omnes voluntatis actiones esse liberas. Et simili quoque modo liberum arbitrium distinguit Celeberrimus Alexander Morus, De Gratia & libero Arbitrio Disp. 1. Thesi 28. Ubi duas proponit definitiones, unam liberi arbitrii latius accepti, alteram vero liberi arbitrii stricte sumpti. Juxta priorem notionem liberum arbitrium ab ipso describitur, Dos intelligentis naturae maxime propria qua nihil vult, aut aversatur, nisi quod esse bonum, aut malum intellexit. Juxta vero posteriorem, voluntas quatenus media post consultationem ab intellectu monstrata eligit.
english: This is the teaching of John Strang, Doctor of Sacred Theology and principal professor at the Academy of Glasgow, in his treatise On the Will and Actions of God concerning Sin (book 3, chapter 14). After setting out and developing what we have described, he says he does not deny that the term free choice is rightly used in that strict sense, though in another and wider sense he maintains that all the will's acts are free.

The famous Alexander More draws the same kind of distinction in his On Grace and Free Choice (disputation 1, thesis 28). He offers two definitions, one of free choice in the wider sense and one of free choice in the strict sense.

In the first sense he describes free choice as "the endowment most proper to an intelligent nature, by which it wills or shuns nothing except what it has understood to be good or evil." In the second, it is "the will as it chooses means set before it by the intellect after deliberation."
